claims.claim: Cohen and Rossing, 'The acoustics of mandolins', Acoust. Sci. & Tech. 24(1), 1-6 (2003) exists (DOI 10.1250/ast.24.1.). Abstract: electronic TV holography on four mandolins and a mandola; lowest (0,0) modes can appear as a triplet (as in a guitar) or as a doublet; modal frequencies correlate with frequency-response curves; sound radiation is quite uniform over 0-5 kHz with some rolloff above 2.5 kHz.
claims.input_file_says: Cohen and Rossing reported that mandolin sound radiation remains fairly uniform from 0 to 5 kHz, with gradual rolloff above 2.5 kHz.
claims.notes: Only the abstract wording was seen, relayed through a search result. The J-STAGE host could not be fetched from this sandbox. The abstract wording supports the file; per-instrument modal tables were NOT read.

claims.claim: The 2000 ASA (139th meeting, Atlanta) lay-language paper by Cohen and Rossing compares two Gibson F-type mandolins, one with an elliptical (oval) sound hole and one with f-holes, by holographic interferometry. It reports a pair of modes in which the plates rock side to side about a central nodal line at 524 and 546 Hz in the f-hole instrument and 579 and 644 Hz in the oval-hole instrument; the weaker bass of the oval-hole instrument is attributed to a larger mismatch between the main air resonance and the lowest plate modes. The figures 318 Hz (f-hole) and 423 Hz (oval) were NOT found in this source.
claims.input_file_says: TV holography found a primary top-plate mode at 318 Hz in an f-hole mandolin, shifting to 423 Hz in an oval-hole mandolin.

claims.claim: The Quintavalla paper exists, but not under the details the file implies. It is: M. Quintavalla, F. Gabrielli, C. Canevari, 'The Acoustics of Traditional Italian Mandolins and Their Relation with Soundboard Wood Properties', International Journal of Wood Culture 2(1-3), 1-18, DOI 10.1163/27723194-bja10001 (listed as March 2022 on ResearchGate; one lab page says 2024). Fragments say: the bowl back is stiff and massive so back-related peaks lie above soundboard modes; soundboard first five eigenmodes were simulated with +-50% elastic-property sensitivity; low-frequency monopole (Helmholtz-type) air modes occur; a mode named WWDF-1 is identified. None of the numerical values in the input file (194.1, 180.3-204.3, 201.1, 553.6, 451.5-694.5, 596.6, 740.5, 697.0, 1035, 106.1 Hz) or the labels T(1,1)_1 etc. could be checked.

claims.claim: Irish bouzouki history: Johnny Moynihan (Sweeney's Men) brought a Greek tetrachordo bouzouki to Ireland and retuned it G2 D3 A3 D4 (GDAD); Andy Irvine also used GDAD from 1971; Irvine gave a Greek bouzouki to Dónal Lunny, who replaced the octave pairs of the two bass courses with unison pairs; English luthier Peter Abnett built the first distinctly 'Irish' bouzouki for Lunny in 1972 (hybrid body, three-piece partly staved back, straight sides); the first flat-backed instrument came from a John Bailey zouk bought by Moynihan in London. GDAD is the most common tuning today.
claims.input_file_says: developed in the 1960s-1970s via Johnny Moynihan, luthier Peter Abnett, and Dónal Lunny.

claims.claim: Brezas et al., 'An Integrated Method for the Vibroacoustic Evaluation of a Carbon Fiber Bouzouki', Applied Sciences 13(7), 4585 (2023), DOI 10.3390/app13074585 exists (Hellenic Mediterranean University; ESPI, FEM, impulse tests; CarbonMusic project). Three carbon-fibre bouzoukis were moulded from a 3D scan of a wooden instrument; C01 was compared with the best of three wooden instruments (W02). Authors include Brezas and Kaselouris.
